title: Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation:  Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning
Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning
summary: Deep learning regression and classification tools typically do not capture model uncertainty, whereas Bayesian models do but at prohibitive computational cost. The paper casts dropout training in neural networks as approximate variational inference in deep Gaussian processes, yielding MC dropout: averaging T stochastic forward passes to estimate predictive mean and variance. On UCI regression benchmarks, notably Boston Housing, MC dropout improves test RMSE and predictive log-likelihood over VI and probabilistic back-propagation, achieving 2.97 ± 0.19 RMSE on Boston Housing in the 20-split setting.

text: Cloning into 'repo'...

why: The authors' repo is cloned and contains the entire experimental apparatus: experiment.py, net/net.py, and all UCI_Datasets directories with data.txt, the exact 20 train/test index splits, dropout_rates.txt, tau_values.txt, n_epochs/n_hidden configs, plus the authors' published result files (test_MC_rmse_100_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt etc.) for direct comparison. Nothing data- or weight-wise is missing (models are trained from scratch). What is broken is the runtime: the code targets Keras 2.2.0 on Theano 0.8.2 (README), Theano is unmaintained and not installable on Python 3.12, TF1.x/Keras 2.2 wheels do not exist for Python 3.12, and 9 of 11 Python files are Python-2 style. So we keep the authors' logic (architecture, dropout rates, epochs, tau/grid-search protocol, per-split train/val selection) but port the training/evaluation core to a modern framework and run the same splits.
est_runtime: Port work: ~20-30 min (rewrite net/net.py + experiment.py training/MC-dropout loop in a modern framework, keep split loading and grid-search logic). Runs (Boston Housing, 1x50 net, 400 epochs, batch 32, per-split grid over the repo's dropout_rates/tau_values, T MC forward passes): ~10-15 s per model fit on 22 CPU cores, so ~2-4 min per split with grid search. Full 20-split C1 protocol is ~40-80 min of compute, i.e. borderline-to-over the ~60 min total budget once the port is included.
scale_down_plan: Keep the exact released protocol but shrink along the split axis, not the model axis: evaluate the first 5 of the 20 released Boston Housing splits (index_train_*/index_test_*), same 1-hidden-layer/50-unit net, same dropout rates, same l=1e-2, same per-split train/val grid over tau, same 10x epochs (400), batch 32, Adam, T MC forward passes. Report mean test RMSE with standard error over 5 splits and state the split count explicitly. Secondary cheap confirmation on Yacht Hydrodynamics (N=308, <1 min/split) if time permits. Expected effect on the number: the point estimate should land near the released 2.83-2.97 range within a much wider error bar (SE roughly sqrt(20/5)~2x larger, i.e. +/-0.3-0.4 instead of +/-0.19); the qualitative claim (MC dropout beats VI, comparable-to-better than PBP 3.01) remains testable, but the printed +/-0.19 cannot be matched with 5 splits. If the port finishes fast, extend toward 10-20 splits; do not cut epochs or MC samples first, since those change the estimator itself.
blockers: code targets Theano 0.8.2 + Keras 2.2.0; Theano is dead and cannot be installed on Python 3.12
Keras 2.2.0 / TensorFlow 1.x have no wheels for Python 3.12 (and Keras 3 API differs: layer-level train-time dropout loops, .compile/.fit behaviour, model saving)
9 of 11 python files are Python-2 style (print statements, old import style) and need 2to3-style edits even before framework porting
no GPU on this machine; README launch command assumes device=gpu + float32 (not fatal: the UCI nets are tiny and the paper reports CPU-class runtimes, e.g. naval 276 s/split incl. BO)
protocol requires a per-split train/val split + grid search over dropout rate and tau before the final train, so per-split cost is much larger than a single 400-epoch fit

approach: This is a partial_release reproduction: we keep the authors' released data and the exact 20 per-split train/test index files from https://github.com/yaringal/DropoutUncertaintyExps (bostonHousing/data/data.txt, index_train_i.txt, index_test_i.txt, dropout_rates.txt, tau_values.txt, n_epochs.txt, n_hidden.txt) and their grid-search-over-dropout-rate-and-tau protocol, but re-implement the 1-hidden-layer/50-unit dropout network plus the MC-dropout training/evaluation loop in PyTorch (CPU) because the original Keras 2.2.0 + Theano 0.8.2 stack and its Python-2 source cannot run on Python 3.12 (this is the single documented deviation from R13). For each of the first 5 of the 20 released Boston Housing splits we carve an 80/20 train/validation split from the training indices, grid-search dropout rate and tau by validation log-likelihood, set the L2 weight decay from the searched tau and l=1e-2 via the eq.(7) relation exactly as coded in net/net.py, train the final model for the fixed epoch budget (10x the base schedule, ~400 epochs, no early stopping) with Adam/batch-32, and evaluate test RMSE (inverse-transformed to original target units) and predictive log-likelihood with T=1000 MC-dropout stochastic forward passes. reproduce.py aggregates mean±standard-error over the 5 splits, writes results/metrics.json, and prints the authors' released per-split result files for direct comparison. The expected point estimate is ~2.83-2.97 (inside the 0.19 tolerance around C1=2.97) but with a roughly 2x wider standard error (5 of 20 splits), so the honest verdict is partially_reproduced.
steps: 1. Environment: verify python>=3.12, numpy/scipy/pandas/scikit-learn present, then `pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu` (CPU wheel) and `python -c "import torch;print(torch.__version__)"`. Do NOT attempt to install Theano/Keras 2.2/TF1 - they are uninstallable on 3.12 (documented blocker; deviation from R13).

2. Repo check: confirm DropoutUncertaintyExps/ is present; assert existence of UCI_Datasets/bostonHousing/data/{data.txt, index_features.txt, index_target.txt, dropout_rates.txt, tau_values.txt, n_epochs.txt, n_hidden.txt, n_splits.txt} and index_train_0..19.txt / index_test_0..19.txt, plus results/ releasing test_MC_rmse_100_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt.

3. Read experiment.py and net/net.py end-to-end; write down (in a notes file or docstring) the exact protocol: how the 80/20 train-val split is formed, how (dropout_rate, tau) are grid-searched and scored, how weight decay lambda is derived from tau/l/N, the exact epoch count and multiplier, and how RMSE and eq.(8) log-likelihood are computed. This dictation of the authors' logic is what the PyTorch port must mirror.
4. Parse the bostonHousing data dir config files and print them (dropout rates, tau values, n_epochs, n_hidden, n_splits, index_features, index_target) so the counts drive the grid size.
5. Write config.py with the values above (paper/assumption tags inline).
6. Write data_utils.py: load_data(split) -> (X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val, X_test, y_test, scaler_y); standardize X and y on train statistics; verbose shapes. No torch import needed here.
7. Write model.py: DropoutRegressor(Q, hidden=50, p_in, p_out) with dropout before each weight layer; keep_dropout_at_eval flag.

8. Write mc_dropout.py: compute_lambda(tau,l,N) reading net/net.py's formula; train_model(...) (Adam lr=1e-3, batch 32, fixed epochs, shuffled); mc_predict(model, X, T=1000) -> mean, variance; rmse_inverse(y, yhat_mean, scaler_y); predictive_log_likelihood(...) per eq.(8)/net.py; grid_search(...) scoring by validation LL.

9. Write reproduce.py: iterate config.full_split_list, run grid search then final train then MC test eval, store per-split results, compute mean and SE = std/sqrt(n), set within_tolerance = |mean - 2.97| <= 0.19, dump results/metrics.json including split count, config snapshot, and the authors' released values.
10. Write compare_with_released.py to read the authors' results/*_100_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt files and print alongside ours.
11. Run the intermediate checks (see intermediate_checks) and fix any that fail before the full run.
12. Smoke test: `python reproduce.py --smoke` (split 0, 2 epochs, T=10, 1 grid point, 64 samples) - assert finite RMSE/LL, correct tensor shapes, <60 s.
13. Full run: `python reproduce.py --dataset bostonHousing --split-count 5` -> 5 splits x (grid search + 10x-epoch final train + T=1000 MC eval).
14. Inspect results/metrics.json: mean RMSE vs 2.97 with tolerance 0.19; compare to the authors' released 2.83/2.90; confirm the printed SE is ~2x the paper's because only 5 of 20 splits are used.
15. If budget remains after the 5-split Boston run, add a cheap secondary confirmation on Yacht Hydrodynamics (N=308), same protocol, and append it to metrics.json.

16. Write a short summary block into results/metrics.json stating the deviation (5/20 splits, grid-search instead of BO, PyTorch instead of Keras/Theano) and the resulting verdict (partially_reproduced).
smoke_test: `python reproduce.py --smoke` runs only split 0 on the first 64 training rows for 2 epochs with T=10 MC forward passes and a single (dropout,tau) grid point; it asserts the data loader returns correctly shaped train/val/test arrays, the net has 751 parameters, training losses are finite and decreasing, MC predictions have shape (n_test,) with non-negative variance, and RMSE/log-likelihood are finite scalars. It writes results/smoke_metrics.json and must finish in under ~60 s, proving the full data->train->MC-eval->JSON flow before the expensive run.
intermediate_checks: Data integrity: data.txt has 506 rows and Q columns equal to index_features.txt; index_train_i.txt and index_test_i.txt are disjoint and their union is all 506 indices; every index is in range.
Split hygiene: the 80/20 validation set is drawn only from training indices, disjoint from the test indices, and reproducible from the fixed seed (A3/A8).
Grid files parse: dropout_rates.txt and tau_values.txt yield the expected number of values (print them); grid size = len(rates)*len(taus).
Parameter count: 13*50+50 + 50*1+1 = 751 parameters; print and assert this matches the instantiated model.

Weight-decay sanity: print lambda for the searched tau values and N=train size; assert lambda > 0 and varies monotonically with tau as eq.(7)/net.py implies; verify lambda matches net/net.py's formula on a hand-computed example.
Target scaling: after standardization the train target has mean~0, std~1; inverse_transform(standardize(y))==y within 1e-8.

Sanity baseline: fit a plain (dropout-off at eval, or a least-squares linear) model on split 0 and confirm test RMSE is in a plausible Boston range (~3-6), i.e. the pipeline is not degenerate before the dropout run.

Authors' anchor: read UCI_Datasets/bostonHousing/results/test_MC_rmse_100_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt and record the released per-split RMSEs (expect point estimate ~2.83-2.97) so our numbers can be compared immediately after the full run.
budget_plan: Total ~60 min. Setup + reading experiment.py/net.py + writing the PyTorch port: ~15-20 min. Intermediate checks: ~5 min. Smoke test: ~1-2 min. Full 5-split Boston Housing run (grid search + 400-epoch final train + T=1000 MC eval, ~2-4 min/split on the CPU cores): ~10-20 min. Aggregation, comparison to released files, and writing results/metrics.json: ~5 min. Remaining ~5-10 min reserved as buffer; if the port finished fast and the buffer is intact, extend the split list toward 10 before considering any reduction of epochs or T (the route forbids shrinking the estimator).

Informs the default batch size so the full 20-split run fits the clean re-run limit.

import time
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.set_num_threads(1)
torch.manual_seed(0)

W1 = torch.randn(13, 50 * 1)  # placeholder; we use nn.Linear below
import torch.nn as nn

def make():
    m = nn.Module()
    m.l1 = nn.Linear(13, 50)
    m.l2 = nn.Linear(50, 1)
    return m

def bench(batch_size, n_steps=2000, n=364, d=13, p=0.05, reg=1.5e-6):
    model = make()
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, eps=1e-7)
    X = torch.randn(n, d)
    y = torch.randn(n)
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(n_steps // (n // batch_size)):
        perm = torch.randperm(n, generator=g)
        for s in range(0, n, batch_size):
            idx = perm[s:s + batch_size]
            h = F.dropout(X[idx], p, training=True)
            h = torch.relu(model.l1(h))
            h = F.dropout(h, p, training=True)
            pred = model.l2(h)
            loss = F.mse_loss(pred.squeeze(-1), y[idx]) + reg * (
                (model.l1.weight ** 2).sum() + (model.l2.weight ** 2).sum())
            opt.zero_grad()
            loss.backward()
            opt.step()
    dt = time.perf_counter() - t0
    steps = (n_steps // (n // batch_size)) * (n // batch_size + (1 if n % batch_size else 0))
    print(f"batch={batch_size}: {dt:.2f}s for {steps} steps -> {1000*dt/steps:.3f} ms/step "
          f"-> per grid point (400 epochs) ~ {400*(n/batch_size)*0.001*dt/steps*1000/0.001:.1f}s")
    return dt / steps

for b in (32, 128):
    bench(b)

"""Loading of the authors' released UCI data, config files and splits [R11].

Everything comes from repo/UCI_Datasets/<dataset>/data/ exactly as consumed by the
authors' experiment.py: data.txt, index_features.txt, index_target.txt,
index_train_<i>.txt / index_test_<i>.txt, dropout_rates.txt, tau_values.txt,
n_epochs.txt, n_hidden.txt, n_splits.txt.
"""
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

from config import UCI_DIR, DATASET_DIRS


def dataset_data_dir(name: str) -> Path:
    return UCI_DIR / DATASET_DIRS[name] / "data"


def dataset_results_dir(name: str) -> Path:
    return UCI_DIR / DATASET_DIRS[name] / "results"


def load_dataset(name: str):
    """Return X, y and the dataset's own config files."""
    d = dataset_data_dir(name)
    data = np.loadtxt(d / "data.txt")
    index_features = np.loadtxt(d / "index_features.txt").astype(int)
    index_target = int(np.loadtxt(d / "index_target.txt"))
    X = data[:, index_features]
    y = data[:, index_target]
    cfg = {
        "n_hidden_units": int(np.loadtxt(d / "n_hidden.txt")),
        "n_epochs_base": int(np.loadtxt(d / "n_epochs.txt")),
        "n_splits": int(np.loadtxt(d / "n_splits.txt")),
        "dropout_rates": [float(v) for v in np.loadtxt(d / "dropout_rates.txt").tolist()],
        "tau_values": [float(v) for v in np.loadtxt(d / "tau_values.txt").tolist()],
        "n_rows": int(data.shape[0]),
        "n_features": int(X.shape[1]),
    }
    return X, y, cfg


def load_split_indices(name: str, split: int):
    d = dataset_data_dir(name)
    index_train = np.loadtxt(d / f"index_train_{split}.txt").astype(int)
    index_test = np.loadtxt(d / f"index_test_{split}.txt").astype(int)
    return index_train, index_test


def check_split_integrity(X, y, index_train, index_test, split: int) -> dict:
    """Data integrity / split hygiene checks (plan intermediate_checks 1-2)."""
    n = X.shape[0]
    it, ie = index_train.tolist(), index_test.tolist()
    info = {
        "split": int(split),
        "n_rows": int(n),
        "n_train": len(it),
        "n_test": len(ie),
        "disjoint": len(set(it) & set(ie)) == 0,
        "union_is_all": len(set(it) | set(ie)) == n,
        "indices_in_range": (min(it) >= 0 and max(it) < n and min(ie) >= 0 and max(ie) < n),
    }
    assert info["disjoint"], f"split {split}: train/test indices overlap"
    assert info["union_is_all"], f"split {split}: train/test indices do not cover all rows"
    assert info["indices_in_range"], f"split {split}: out-of-range indices"
    return info


def carve_validation(index_train, val_fraction: float):
    """Last 20% of the training rows become the validation set, as in
    repo/experiment.py lines 132-136 (deterministic, no shuffling)."""
    n_sub = int(val_fraction * index_train.shape[0])
    return index_train[:n_sub], index_train[n_sub:]


class Standardizer:
    """Standardize X and y on the training subset (net.py normalize=True)."""

    def __init__(self, X_train, y_train):
        self.mean_X = X_train.mean(axis=0)
        std_X = X_train.std(axis=0)
        std_X[std_X == 0] = 1.0  # net.py line 53
        self.std_X = std_X
        self.mean_y = float(y_train.mean())
        self.std_y = float(y_train.std())

    def transform_X(self, X):
        return (X - self.mean_X) / self.std_X

    def transform_y(self, y):
        return (y - self.mean_y) / self.std_y

    def inverse_y(self, y):
        return y * self.std_y + self.mean_y

"""Core ported logic: repo/experiment.py + repo/net/net.py, in PyTorch.

Mirrored protocol per split (experiment.py):
  1. validation set = last 20% of the training rows
  2. grid search over (dropout_rate, tau) from the repo's data files; each candidate
     net is trained on the (train - validation) subset and scored by MC-dropout
     log-likelihood on the validation set
  3. a fresh net is trained on the ENTIRE training set with the best (dropout, tau)
  4. test MC RMSE (eq. 6) and test predictive log-likelihood (eq. 8) are reported

Mirrored maths (net.py):
  weight decay  reg = lengthscale^2 * (1 - dropout) / (2 * N * tau)      (eq. 7)
  MC prediction T stochastic forward passes averaged                     (eq. 6)
  log-likelihood logsumexp_t[-0.5*tau*(y - Yt_hat)^2] - log T - 0.5 log 2pi + 0.5 log tau
  (eq. 8, computed in ORIGINAL target units with the searched tau)
"""
import math
import zlib

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

from model import DropoutNet

DTYPE = torch.float64


def stable_seed(*parts) -> int:
    """Deterministic, order-independent seed for a training/eval call."""
    return zlib.crc32("|".join(str(p) for p in parts).encode("utf-8")) & 0x7FFFFFFF


def l2_reg_coeff(tau: float, dropout: float, n_train: int, lengthscale: float) -> float:
    """net.py line 72: reg = lengthscale**2 * (1 - dropout) / (2 * N * tau)."""
    return lengthscale ** 2 * (1.0 - dropout) / (2.0 * n_train * tau)


def _to_tensor(a):
    return torch.as_tensor(np.asarray(a, dtype=np.float64), dtype=DTYPE)


def train_net(Xn, yn, n_hidden, dropout, tau, n_epochs, batch_size, lengthscale,
              seed, lr, adam_eps):
    """One training run exactly as net.net(): Adam on MSE + reg*||W||^2 on kernels.

    Xn/yn are already standardized (net.py normalize=True).  Deterministic: the
    global torch RNG is re-seeded at the start of every call, so results do not
    depend on execution order or on sequential vs. parallel execution.
    """
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    Xn = _to_tensor(Xn)
    yn = _to_tensor(yn)
    n = Xn.shape[0]
    reg = l2_reg_coeff(tau, dropout, n, lengthscale)
    model = DropoutNet(Xn.shape[1], n_hidden, dropout)
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr, eps=adam_eps)
    g = torch.Generator()
    g.manual_seed((seed + 1) & 0x7FFFFFFF)
    for _ in range(int(n_epochs)):
        perm = torch.randperm(n, generator=g)
        for s in range(0, n, batch_size):
            idx = perm[s:s + batch_size]
            pred = model(Xn[idx])
            loss = F.mse_loss(pred, yn[idx]) + reg * model.l2_penalty()
            opt.zero_grad()
            loss.backward()
            opt.step()
    return model


def mc_forward_passes(model, Xn, T, chunk):
    """T stochastic forward passes with dropout active, vectorised over T.

    nn.Linear/F.dropout accept (B, n, d) batches, so the same ``forward`` code path
    is used for training and for MC prediction (T forward passes, eq. 6).
    """
    n = Xn.shape[0]
    hidden = sum(lin.out_features for lin in model.layers)
    per_chunk = max(1, int(chunk // max(1, n * hidden)))
    outs = []
    done = 0
    while done < T:
        b = min(per_chunk, T - done)
        xb = Xn.unsqueeze(0).expand(b, n, Xn.shape[1])
        with torch.no_grad():
            outs.append(model(xb))  # (b, n) in standardized units
        done += b
    return torch.cat(outs, dim=0)  # (T, n)


def predict(model, Xn, T, seed, chunk=4e6):
    """net.py predict(): T stochastic passes; also return a single-pass prediction."""
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    Xn = _to_tensor(Xn)
    Yt = mc_forward_passes(model, Xn, T, chunk)          # (T, n)
    return Yt


def mc_rmse(y_true, Yt_orig):
    """RMSE of the MC-averaged prediction, in original target units (eq. 6)."""
    y = _to_tensor(y_true)
    mc_pred = Yt_orig.mean(dim=0)
    return float(torch.sqrt(((y - mc_pred) ** 2).mean()).item())


def single_pass_rmse(y_true, Yt_orig):
    """net.py 'standard_pred' RMSE: one stochastic forward pass (dropout active)."""
    y = _to_tensor(y_true)
    return float(torch.sqrt(((y - Yt_orig[0]) ** 2).mean()).item())


def predictive_log_likelihood(y_true, Yt_orig, tau, T):
    """net.py lines 134-136: eq. (8) MC approximation, original units, searched tau."""
    y = _to_tensor(y_true)
    a = -0.5 * tau * (y.unsqueeze(0) - Yt_orig) ** 2
    ll = (torch.logsumexp(a, dim=0) - math.log(T) - 0.5 * math.log(2.0 * math.pi)
          + 0.5 * math.log(tau))
    return float(ll.mean().item())


def evaluate(model, X, y, stdizer, tau, T, seed, chunk=4e6):
    """Test/val evaluation in original units: MC RMSE, single-pass RMSE, LL."""
    Xn = stdizer.transform_X(X)
    Yt = predict(model, Xn, T, seed, chunk)              # (T, n) standardized units
    Yt_orig = Yt * stdizer.std_y + stdizer.mean_y        # inverse transform (net.py 129)
    return {
        "mc_rmse": mc_rmse(y, Yt_orig),
        "single_pass_rmse": single_pass_rmse(y, Yt_orig),
        "ll": predictive_log_likelihood(y, Yt_orig, tau, T),
        "mc_pred_mean": Yt_orig.mean(dim=0).cpu().numpy(),
        "mc_var": (Yt_orig.var(dim=0, unbiased=False) +
                   stdizer.std_y ** 2 / tau).cpu().numpy(),  # epistemic + noise var
    }

     protocol, 400 epochs (n_epochs.txt=40 x 10, the Table-1 "10x more iterations"
     setting), batch 32, Adam, T=10000 MC-dropout passes; writes results/metrics.json.

Useful flags:
    --dataset bostonHousing|concrete|energy|yacht|wine|power|kin8nm|naval|protein
    --splits N        first N released splits (default: all released splits)
    --epochx 100      the 10x-more-epochs-again setting (100 x 40 = 4000 epochs; slow)
    --batch-size 128  the released code's batch size (paper text says 32 -> default)
    --workers N       parallel splits (default: cpu_count-1; 0 = sequential)
    --smoke           tiny end-to-end data-flow check, writes results/smoke_metrics.json
"""

import json
import math
import os
import time

import numpy as np
import torch

def intermediate_checks(dataset):

          f"features={cfg['n_features']} target=1")
    print(f"[check] n_epochs.txt={cfg['n_epochs_base']} n_hidden.txt="
          f"{cfg['n_hidden_units']} n_splits.txt={cfg['n_splits']}")
    print(f"[check] dropout_rates.txt={cfg['dropout_rates']} "
          f"tau_values.txt={cfg['tau_values']} -> grid size "
          f"{len(cfg['dropout_rates']) * len(cfg['tau_values'])} per split")

    idx_tr, idx_te = load_split_indices(dataset, 0)
    info = check_split_integrity(X, y, idx_tr, idx_te, 0)
    print(f"[check] split 0: train={info['n_train']} test={info['n_test']} "
          f"disjoint={info['disjoint']} union_is_all={info['union_is_all']}")

    # parameter count (13*50+50 + 50*1+1 = 751 for Boston)
    model = DropoutNet(cfg["n_features"], [cfg["n_hidden_units"]] * config.N_HIDDEN_LAYERS,
                       0.05)
    expected = sum((a * b + b) for a, b in
                   zip([cfg["n_features"]] + [cfg["n_hidden_units"]] * config.N_HIDDEN_LAYERS,
                       [cfg["n_hidden_units"]] * config.N_HIDDEN_LAYERS + [1]))
    print(f"[check] network parameters={model.n_params()} (expected {expected})")
    assert model.n_params() == expected, "parameter count mismatch"

    # weight-decay sanity: lambda from tau/l/N per net.py, monotone in tau
    for tau in cfg["tau_values"]:
        lam = l2_reg_coeff(tau, 0.05, info["n_train"], config.PRIOR_LENGTHSCALE)
        print(f"[check] l2 reg coeff (tau={tau}, p=0.05, N={info['n_train']}, "
              f"l={config.PRIOR_LENGTHSCALE}) = {lam:.3e}")
        assert lam > 0
    lams = [l2_reg_coeff(t, 0.05, info["n_train"], config.PRIOR_LENGTHSCALE)
            for t in cfg["tau_values"]]
    assert all(lams[i] > lams[i + 1] for i in range(len(lams) - 1)), \
        "lambda must decrease monotonically with tau (eq. 7)"

    # target scaling: standardize -> inverse transform must round-trip

          f"std={std.transform_y(y[sub]).std():.6f}; inverse round-trip OK")
    print(f"[check] validation set = last {len(val)} of {len(idx_tr)} training rows "
          f"(val_fraction={config.VAL_FRACTION}, experiment.py lines 132-136)")
    return X, y, cfg


def released_reference(dataset, epoch_multiplier):

"""Print the authors' released per-split results next to ours (fidelity check).

Reads repo/UCI_Datasets/<dataset>/results/*_100_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt (the
authors' released grid-search run) and results/metrics.json (our port), and prints
them side by side.  Read-only diagnostic; never writes anything.
"""
import json

import numpy as np

import config
from data_utils import dataset_results_dir


def main(dataset="bostonHousing", epoch_multiplier=100):
    rdir = dataset_results_dir(dataset)
    ours_path = config.RESULTS_DIR / "metrics.json"
    files = {
        "released MC RMSE": f"test_MC_rmse_{epoch_multiplier}_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt",
        "released LL": f"test_ll_{epoch_multiplier}_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt",
        "released tau": f"test_tau_{epoch_multiplier}_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt",
    }
    released = {}
    for label, fname in files.items():
        p = rdir / fname
        if p.exists():
            released[label] = np.loadtxt(p).tolist()
        else:
            print(f"[warn] missing {p}")
            released[label] = None

    ours = None
    if ours_path.exists():
        ours = json.load(open(ours_path))
        per_split = {r["split"]: r for r in ours["per_split"]}

    n = max(len(v) for v in released.values() if v) if released else 0
    print(f"{'split':>5} | {'rel MC RMSE':>11} | {'our MC RMSE':>11} | "
          f"{'rel LL':>9} | {'our LL':>9} | {'rel tau':>7} | {'our tau':>7} | {'our p':>6}")
    for i in range(n):
        def g(label, j):
            v = released[label]
            return f"{v[j]:11.4f}" if v and j < len(v) else f"{'-':>11}"
        if ours and i in per_split:
            r = per_split[i]
            our_rmse, our_ll, our_tau, our_p = (f"{r['test_mc_rmse']:11.4f}",
                                                f"{r['test_ll']:9.4f}",
                                                f"{r['best_tau']:7.3f}",
                                                f"{r['best_dropout']:6.3f}")
        else:
            our_rmse = our_ll = our_tau = our_p = "-"
        print(f"{i:>5} | {g('released MC RMSE', i)} | {our_rmse} | "
              f"{g('released LL', i)} | {our_ll} | {g('released tau', i)} | "
              f"{our_tau} | {our_p}")

    for label in ("released MC RMSE", "released LL"):
        v = released.get(label)
        if v:
            v = np.asarray(v, dtype=float)
            print(f"{label}: mean {v.mean():.4f} +- {v.std()/np.sqrt(len(v)):.4f} "
                  f"(std error over {len(v)} splits)")
    if ours:
        s = ours["summary"]
        print(f"our MC RMSE: mean {s['mean_mc_rmse']:.4f} +- "
              f"{s['std_error_mc_rmse']:.4f} (std error over {s['n_splits_used']} splits)")
        print(f"our LL:      mean {s['mean_test_ll']:.4f} +- "
              f"{s['std_error_test_ll']:.4f}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import argparse
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--dataset", default="bostonHousing")
    ap.add_argument("--epochx", type=int, default=100)
    args = ap.parse_args()
    main(args.dataset, args.epochx)

def carve_validation(index_train, val_fraction: float):
    """Split the released training indices into (training, validation) EXACTLY as
    repo/experiment.py lines 132-136:

        num_training_examples = int(0.8 * n_train)      # 364 for Boston (n_train=455)
        X_validation = X_train[num_training_examples:]  # the REMAINING last 91 rows
        X_train      = X_train[0:num_training_examples] # the FIRST 364 rows

    Deterministic (no shuffling).  Returns (index_train_sub, index_val, audit).

    Audit (v2 fix): an earlier version of this function returned the two index sets
    swapped (91-row 'train' / 364-row 'val'); the disjointness/size audit below is
    what pins the split down to the authors' one.
    """
    n = int(index_train.shape[0])
    n_train_sub = int((1.0 - val_fraction) * n)   # training rows: first int(0.8*n)
    index_sub = index_train[:n_train_sub]
    index_val = index_train[n_train_sub:]
    overlap = sorted(set(index_sub.tolist()) & set(index_val.tolist()))
    audit = {
        "n_train": int(index_sub.shape[0]),
        "n_val": int(index_val.shape[0]),
        "n_train_total": n,
        "overlap": len(overlap),
        "disjoint": len(overlap) == 0,
        "rule": "training = first int(0.8*n_train) rows, "
                "validation = remaining int(0.2*n_train) rows (experiment.py 132-136)",
    }
    assert audit["disjoint"], f"training/validation index sets overlap on {overlap[:5]}"
    assert audit["n_train"] + audit["n_val"] == n, "train+val != all training rows"
    assert audit["n_train"] > audit["n_val"], "train/val sizes swapped?"
    return index_sub, index_val, audit

def __init__(self, n_in: int, n_hidden, dropout):
        """``dropout`` is either a single rate shared by every dropout layer (the
        released code's grid-search protocol) or a per-weight-layer sequence, e.g.
        [0.05, 0.005] = paper probabilities on input->hidden / hidden->output."""
        super().__init__()
        dims = [n_in] + [int(h) for h in n_hidden] + [1]
        n_layers = len(dims) - 1
        if isinstance(dropout, (int, float)):
            probs = [float(dropout)] * n_layers
        else:
            probs = [float(p) for p in dropout]
        assert len(probs) == n_layers, (
            f"need {n_layers} dropout probabilities (one per weight layer), got {probs}")
        assert all(0.0 <= p < 1.0 for p in probs), f"invalid dropout rates {probs}"
        self.dropout_probs = probs
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList(
            [nn.Linear(dims[i], dims[i + 1]) for i in range(n_layers)]
        )

audit_summary: The clean re-run of `python reproduce.py` (518.9 s, 20 workers on the released Boston splits) deterministically reproduced results/metrics.json: MC-dropout test RMSE 3.0059 +- 0.1732 vs the paper's 2.97 +- 0.19 (|delta|=0.04, inside the 0.19 tolerance) and vs the authors' own released 20-split file 2.9036 +- 0.1768. Nothing was scaled down: despite the router's 5-split forecast and ledger A19, the run used all 20/20 released splits, the 400-epoch (40x10) budget, batch 32, Adam, T=10000 MC passes and the full per-split hyperparameter grid; only the search procedure differs (released 12-point dropout x tau grid scored by validation MC log-likelihood instead of the paper's 40-iteration Spearmint BO, and one shared grid-searched dropout rate rather than the fixed 0.05/0.005 pair), which is what makes R2 and R4 only partial. No number is hardcoded or echoed: per-split RMSEs come from actual from-scratch training (median 2.73, IQR 2.41-3.34), the full grid logs are stored, and paper_numbers_found_in_code is empty. Evaluation is genuine held-out test RMSE in original target units on the authors' official split files with a deterministic last-20%-of-train validation carve, and the residual 0.04 offset is consistent with the unspecified hyperparameters/seeds logged in the assumption ledger. Main fidelity caveats are the R2 dropout-rate scheme, the R4 BO substitution, and the R13 PyTorch-vs-Keras port; none of them changes the dataset, metric, task or proposed method, so no anti-cheat or wrong-experiment flags apply.

Dropout is applied before every weight layer (model.DropoutNet.forward: F.dropout before each Linear), but the run that produced the number uses the released-repo protocol of ONE shared rate per split grid-searched over {0.005,0.01,0.05,0.1} (selected: 0.05 x5, 0.005 x3, 0.01 x7, 0.1 x5 splits), not the paper's fixed 0.05/0.005 pair. A --dropout-mode paper option implements 0.05/0.005 per layer but was not used (ledger A23).

mc_dropout.l2_reg_coeff = l^2*(1-p)/(2*N*tau) (net/net.py, eq. 7) with l=1e-2, N = rows of the fit, applied as reg*||W_kernel||^2 added to MSE; intermediate_checks asserts positivity and monotone decrease in tau.

No Spearmint BO: the authors' released grid search (dropout_rates {0.005,0.01,0.05,0.1} x tau_values {0.1,0.15,0.2} = 12 fits per split) scored by validation MC log-likelihood replaces the 40-iteration BO (ledger A18). The tau grid is far narrower than a log-uniform BO range and the same grid is reused for all splits; disclosed in config.py, metrics.json notes and A18.

n_epochs = n_epochs.txt(40) x 10 = 400, applied to every grid fit and the final refit; printed per split ('n_epochs=400') and recorded in metrics.json. Epoch-multiplier choice (10 vs released 100) documented in A15.
batch_size=32 (paper), Adam lr=1e-3 eps=1e-7, minibatch loop in train_net; printed 'batch=32' for each split.
config.PRIOR_LENGTHSCALE = 1e-2 used in the weight-decay coefficient and reported in metrics.json config.

evaluate() -> mc_forward_passes performs T=10000 dropout-active stochastic passes (vectorised, Keras training=True semantics), averages them (eq. 6) and computes test RMSE in original units after std_y/mean_y inverse transform.
predictive_log_likelihood implements logsumexp(-0.5*tau*(y-yhat)^2) - log T - 0.5log(2pi) + 0.5log(tau) (eq. 8, the paper's -1/2 log tau^-1 = +1/2 log tau), giving -2.4941 +- 0.0480 over 20 splits.

config.EARLY_STOPPING=False; train_net runs a fixed 400 epochs with no validation-based stopping; metrics.json records early_stopping: false.
